PUC DOCKET NO. 59475
JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR            BEFORE THE STATE OFFICE OF
ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY
LLC AND LCRA TSC TO AMEND THEIR 
CERTIFICATES OF CONVENIENCE AND   ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS
NECESSITY FOR THE BELL COUNTY EAST SWITCH TO BIG HILL SUBSTATION TRANSMISSION LINE
IN BELL, BURNET, CONCHO, CORYELL,
LAMPASAS, LLANO, MASON,
MCCULLOCH, MENARD, MILAM, MILLS, SAN SABA, SCHLEICHER, TOM GREEN, AND WILLIAMSON COUNTIES
INTERVENOR ASHLEY GULBRANSON INITIAL POST-HEARING BRIEF
TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
Ashley Gulbranson, pro se intervenor, respectfully submits this Initial Post-Hearing Brief in PUC Docket Number 59475 to the State Office of Administrative Hearings ("SOAH") Administrative Law Judges ("ALJs") regarding Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC’s (“Oncor’s”) and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation’s (“LCRA’s”) (collectively, “Applicants”) application for a certificate of convenience and necessity (“CCN”) for Bell County East to Bill Hill 765-kV transmission line. The deadline for the parties to file post-hearing initial briefs is June 19,2026. Therefore, this brief is timely filed.  
   I, Ashley Gulbranson, respectfully request that the Administrative Law Judges recommend DENIAL of the Joint Application (the "Application") of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation (the "Applicants") in its entirety. I respectfully ask that you do not give the Applicants the authority of eminent domain on the hardworking landowners of the beautiful Central Texas hill country based on an application that is so lacking in every regard.
1. INTRODUCTION AND STATEMENT OF POSITION
I, Ashley Gulbranson, pro se intervenor, route links G71, G72, G73, am one of approximately 1,400 landowners that were notified of the application after March 26, 2026. I am a homeschool mom of four. I have no prior knowledge of things like filing on the interchange, preparing testimony, making motions, responding to the court, submitting evidence, briefs, and the list goes on and on. I have been given a very short time frame to learn and decipher a process that is completely new to me. This condensed timeline along with the inability to secure legal representation has greatly restricted my ability to properly understand, prepare for, and participate in these proceedings. The requirements that are associated with the Public Utility Commission proceedings are ones that are completely unfamiliar to an ordinary landowner like myself. Unlike the Applicants, Commission Staff, and parties who have routinely participated in these proceedings as their profession, we, as affected landowners, have attempted to defend our homes, our property rights, and our family’s future while simultaneously continuing daily in responsibilities, maintaining employment, and attending to family responsibilities. The condensed procedural schedule has greatly limited my ability to adequately understand requirements and filings, to prepare testimony, and participate in this process meaningfully. This situation has only been made harder because many of the qualified attorneys familiar with Public Utility Commission litigation have already been retained by others involved in the proceeding, making legal representation unavailable to many landowners like myself. In my opinion, this whole process has created a significant disadvantage for us ordinary landowners, and it has hindered meaningful participation as well as due process protections that should be offered in proceedings of this consequence and significance. 

This proceeding regards one of the largest transmission projects to ever be proposed in the State of Texas. Administrative Law Judges have stated this is the largest and most complex project the State Office of Administrative Hearings has ever seen.  The Applicants, with no shortage of resources, highly experienced lawyers, and hundreds of experts are seeking authority to construct 765-kV transmission line infrastructure across hundreds of miles of private property and imposing the astronomical costs upon Texas ratepayers. This will cause grave effects to thousands of landowners like myself and my neighbors. We ask that you work with those who spend their lives working the very land the Applicants are seeking to take.

The authority sought by Applicants is exceptional, including the power of eminent domain, the ability to permanently change and burden private property with line easements, as well as the ability to transfer substantial project costs to the citizens of Texas. The privilege of exceptional authority comes with exceptional responsibility, as a result the burden imposed upon the Applicants is significant.

The Applicants have a responsibility to prove compliance with all Commission rules, all statutory requirements, and basic Texas and U.S. constitutional rights of private citizens. Applicants must show compliance with the public participation and notification requirements established by the Commission. Applicants have a lot to prove before taking land from the rural hardworking ratepayers of Texas.  

I, Ashley Gulbranson, am requesting that the Administrative Law Judges (ALJ’s) recommend denial of the Application, and the Commission should deny the requested Certificate of Convenience and Necessity as the due process of almost 1,400 land and property owners has been violated for reasons to follow:
• Failure to comply and provide proper notice under 16 TAC §22.52
• Failure to provide meaningful public participation opportunities
• Failure to adequately identify and evaluate community values








II. SUMMARY OF GROUNDS FOR DENIAL

This information supports denial of the Application for the following independent reasons:

A. Failure to comply and provide proper notice under 16 TAC §22.52
Applicants have failed to provide proper notification to all landowners who would be affected by the eventual application by removing the opportunity to attend a public meeting, as required by TAC 22.52.
Applicants failure to give notice of a public meeting to the almost 1,400 affected landowners took away their chance for participation in said meeting.
Applicants have not satisfied the letter and intent of 16 TAC §22.52. This rule is there to ensure that all affected landowners who will receive an application also receive the opportunity for meaningful participation before any route selections or decisions are settled. Approximately one-third of landowners affected have been denied this opportunity.
On day five of the hearing on merits  (Friday June 12, 2026), during a cross examination by Erik Gulbranson, Commissioner McAdams was asked, “based on Texas Admin Code 22.52 (5)…without written notice for a public meeting, a day-for-day extension is required, shouldn’t the almost 1,400 landowners, like myself and my family, who were added after the meeting and not given notice, be given said extensions?” And the Commissioner answered, “…So if they did not follow each condition of the Texas Administrative Code, which you sited, no. You have grounds for extension, and basically, re-notice.”



B. Failure to provide meaningful public participation opportunities

• Applicants then added approximately 400 miles of new route links after the June 2025 public meetings. Lack of notice of public meeting removed the ability to contribute to community values, habitable structures, concerns, as well as other valuable information in the same way the originally notified were for those new properties listed.
• The number of properties affected by this project jumped from approximately 2,800 to approximately 4,200 after these changes.
• Even with these substantial changes, Applicants lacked the execution of any additional public meetings as required by TAC 22.52 (4) (a). When asked in her testimony what the purpose of the public participation meetings were, Casey Petty answered “The purpose of the public participation meetings was to solicit comments and input from residents, landowners, public officials, and other interested parties concerning the Proposed Transmission Line Project and the overall 
transmission line routing process.  Such meetings help ensure that the values and concerns of the public are adequately identified and considered.  Additionally, Applicants utilized the public meeting process as an opportunity to provide information about the Proposed Transmission Line 
Project, including the need for the project and the certification process.” [emphasis added]





C. Failure to Properly Evaluate Community Values
At the SOAH hearing held June 8 – 12, 2026, Applicants repeatedly testified that public participation meetings are critical for identifying community values. However, Applicants have chosen to deny approximately 1,400 landowners any opportunity to participate in those meetings. Applicants have presented little proof that community values have been compared or incorporated into any route selection.


II. Argument

Public participation is a key proponent in The Commission's routing process. If affected landowners are not informed that a project even exists, public participation cannot occur. Applicants have admitted by their own testimony the project expanded after June 2025 public meetings. However, they failed to provide approximately 1,400 newly affected landowners the same participation opportunity as those notified. This failure greatly weakens the integrity of the process as it deprived almost 1,400 landowners their rightly owed opportunity to give information on community values, routing constraints, and prudent avoidance considerations.

At the time of the public meetings conducted in June 2026, approximately 2,800 property owners were invited to participate. These people had been identified as affected landowners that would receive notice of application. Applicants repeatedly testified throughout this proceeding that public meetings serve a critical function in route development and route refinement. Applicants informed that public meetings were intended to gather community values, obtain local knowledge from landowners, identify residences and habitable structures, and improve route selection. The Commission recognizes the importance of these public meetings. That is why they require them. Public participation is a key and necessary component of the routing process. However, the project that was presented in the March 26, 2026 application differed from the project presented during the June 2025 public meetings. Over 400 miles of new alternative routes had been added. During her testimony, Casey Petty testified that route link modifications were made after the public participation meetings.

This shows that after the completion of the June 2025 public meetings, Applicants had removed approximately 140 miles of route links, modified approximately 68 miles of route links, added approximately 400 miles of brand-new route links, increasing the affected properties from approximately 2,800 to approximately 4,200. These aren’t minor adjustments! These changes fundamentally changed the number of affected landowners. The addition of approximately 400 miles of route links is a significant route modification. However, Applicants chose to host no additional meetings.

The landowners who were not granted the rightfully due public meeting never had the opportunity to identify community values, ask questions, review route alternatives, meet with project representatives, provide local knowledge, and retain legal counsel during early stages of project. Approximately one-third of all affected landowners were denied that which was given to every landowner notified in June of 2025 during the public meetings. When Mr. Marusak was asked by pro se intervenor Ben Tanner on day one of the hearing on merits held June 8-12, 2026 “Was early landowner feedback a factor in the removal of some of the links that were removed?” Mr. Marusak answered, “yes, sir”. It would not be reasonable for the Commission to say the public meeting requirements have been satisfied when one-third of the affected landowners never had the opportunity to participate in them. Applicants cannot argue they have exceeded what was required when approximately 1,400 affected landowners had participation withheld from them. If public participation is valuable enough to require a public meeting, then all affected landowners need the opportunity to do so.

Approximately 1,400 affected landowners only became aware of this project when they received the application after March 26, 2026. These landowners were immediately at a disadvantage through no fault of their own.  In OPUC Initial Brief regarding the un-notified landowners it is stated, “…their general opposition should not be disregarded simply because they could not meet the cumbersome procedural requirements to have their individual voice heard. This is especially true considering the condensed timeline driven by the statutory deadline for a final commission determination.” They entered the process late, no chance to contribute before routes were established, and no knowledgeable attorneys to be found. This is exactly why meaningful notification is required before an application – to ensure a fair process for all affected. Applicants have repeatedly argued that compliance with 16 TAC §22.52(a)(4) was satisfied because public meetings were conducted in June 2025, but this argument ignores the broader purpose and intent of the rule. 16 TAC §22.52(a)(4) purpose is clear, “The utility must hold at least one public meeting prior to the filing if 25 or more persons would be entitled to receive direct mail notice of the application.”  The purpose of TAC 22.52 (a)(4) is to create a meaningful opportunity to participate for all landowners. The added approximately 1,400 landowners on the added 400 miles of alternative routes are entitled to the opportunity to participate in one public meeting. The need for public participation is great when routing major transmission lines, especially ones new to Texas.

Approximately 1,400 landowners have lost the opportunity to identify community values, lost months of time to prepare, lost access to experienced legal counsel, lost opportunity to influence route development, and lost the opportunity to provide valuable local information. These harms are relevant and are directly attributed to the Applicants' failure to provide equal participation opportunities. OPUC even states in their initial brief, “during the hearing, several intervenors complained of difficulties with notice and opportunities to participate prior to hearing… certain persons were not given notice of public participation meetings because no preliminary routes ran within 520 feet of their properties. He continues that after such meetings were held, as a result of route modifications, the properties of then un-noticed persons came to be impacted. The Applicants did not host a public meeting for these newly impacted landowners. In considering final routing determination, OPUC urges the ALJs to consider that this asymmetry of input placed some parties, including those who may not have had the ability to retain counsel, in a difficult position in the lead up to the hearing.” [emphasis added]

However, the Commission has the authority to ensure fairness and protect the public interest.
Landowners who were denied participation opportunities should receive relief. The evidence supports that newly affected landowners lost approximately 206 days of participation opportunity compared to those invited to the June 2025 public meetings. Accordingly, the Commission should provide 206 day-for-day relief or deny the Application.



III. CONCLUSION

The United States Constitution and The Texas Constitution guarantee fundamental due process protections. Among those protections are an opportunity to be heard, proper notice, and an opportunity to present evidence. These protections become especially important when governmental action may result in the taking of private property through eminent domain. Due process concerns are relevant for affected landowners who are not provided timely notice and meaningful participation opportunities. I respectfully ask the Commission to not authorize a project of this scope when a substantial number of affected Texas landowners have been denied equal participation opportunities afforded to others.

The authority sought by Applicants ultimately depends upon the power of eminent domain.
Accordingly, Constitutional protections are particularly important. The Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution and Article I of the Texas Constitution protect citizens from deprivation of property without due process of law. The due process protections that have been violated in this proceeding include proper notice, an opportunity to be heard, and fundamental fairness. The Commission is not merely selecting a route, the Commission is deciding whether private property will ultimately be condemned for the benefit of this project. Since eminent domain authority may follow the Commission's decision, strict adherence to notice and participation requirements is essential.

IV. REQUESTED RELIEF

For the foregoing reasons, I, Ashley Gulbranson pro se intervenor, respectfully request that the Administrative Law Judges recommend denial of the Joint Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation.

If the Commission declines to deny the Application, then I, Ashley Gulbranson pro se intervenor, alternately request: required public meetings for all newly affected landowners, granted day-for-day relief equal to the opportunities denied to approximately 1,400 landowners, preserve all Constitutional, procedural, statutory, and due process objections, as well as issue any and all further relief intervenors that may be justly entitled.

Respectfully submitted June 19, 2026

/s/ Ashley Gulbranson
